# Noise channels and error budgets {#sec-noise}

{{< include _macros.qmd >}}

In the previous chapter, we described in words what can go wrong in a quantum device,
its noise (@sec-noise-sources). In this chapter, we describe noise
mathematically. The goal is to model how noise affects the results of a computation,
and to use these models in our estimates and simulations. One model runs through
the whole chapter: a noisy operation is the ideal operation followed by a *quantum
channel*, a map that turns the state of the qubits into a noisier one.

By the end of the chapter, you should be able to write a channel with Kraus operators
and work out what it does to Pauli expectation values; relate $T_1$, $T_2^*$ and
$T_2$ to the channels behind them; tell local from global noise, and coherent from incoherent errors;
model readout errors; estimate how much signal a circuit keeps; and separate the bias
caused by noise from shot noise.

## Density matrices and channels {#sec-channels}

We first review the two tools that the rest of the chapter uses throughout. If you know
them well, skim this section for the notation.

### Mixed states {#sec-mixed-states}

Noise makes the state of a device uncertain. If the qubits are in the state
$\ket{\psi_k}$ with probability $p_k$, the expectation value of an observable $O$ is
$$
\sum_k p_k \bra{\psi_k}O\ket{\psi_k} = \Tr[O\rho], \qquad \text{with} \quad
\rho = \sum_k p_k \ket{\psi_k}\bra{\psi_k} .
$$
The probability of each measurement outcome is the expectation value of a projector, so
all predictions depend on the ensemble only through $\rho$.

::: {#def-density-matrix}
## Density matrix
A [density matrix]{.gloss key="density-matrix"} on $n$ qubits is a $2^n\times 2^n$
matrix $\rho$ that is positive semidefinite (Hermitian, with no negative eigenvalues)
and has trace one. The expectation value of an observable $O$ is
$\langle O\rangle = \Tr[O\rho]$. A pure state $\ket{\psi}$ has
$\rho = \ket{\psi}\bra{\psi}$, and then $\langle O\rangle = \bra{\psi}O\ket{\psi}$.
Every other state is [mixed]{.gloss key="mixed-state"}.
:::

A density matrix is pure exactly when $\rho^2 = \rho$, or, equivalently, when
$\Tr[\rho^2] = 1$. The [purity]{.gloss key="purity"} $\Tr[\rho^2]$ measures how mixed a
state is. The eigenvalues $\lambda_k$ of $\rho$ are non-negative and sum to one, and the
purity is $\sum_k\lambda_k^2$. It is 1 when one eigenvalue is 1 and the others are 0,
which is a pure state. It is smallest, $2^{-n}$, when all $2^n$ eigenvalues are equal,
which is the *maximally mixed state* $I/2^n$: the qubits are in a uniformly random basis
state, and we know nothing about them.

For a single qubit, we want to extend the Bloch-sphere picture of pure states
(@fig-prx) to mixed states. Every Hermitian $2\times 2$ matrix can be written in the
Pauli basis $I, X, Y, Z$, with real coefficients. The Pauli matrices have trace zero,
and the product of two different ones is the third, up to a factor
(@sec-pauli-rotations), so $\Tr[PQ] = 2$ if $P = Q$ and $0$ otherwise. If we write
$\rho = \frac{1}{2}(c_I I + c_x X + c_y Y + c_z Z)$, the trace of $P\rho$ therefore picks
out one coefficient at a time: $c_I = \Tr[\rho] = 1$ and $c_x = \Tr[X\rho] = \langle X\rangle$,
and likewise for $y$ and $z$. A density matrix of one qubit is therefore
$$
\rho = \frac{1}{2}\left(I + r_x X + r_y Y + r_z Z\right), \qquad
r_x = \langle X\rangle,\ r_y = \langle Y\rangle,\ r_z = \langle Z\rangle .
$$ {#eq-bloch}
The vector $\vec r = (r_x, r_y, r_z)$ is the [Bloch vector]{.gloss key="bloch-vector"}.
The matrix $r_x X + r_y Y + r_z Z$ squares to $|\vec r|^2 I$, since the Pauli matrices
anticommute. The eigenvalues of $\rho$ are therefore $(1\pm|\vec r|)/2$, and $\rho$ is a density
matrix exactly when $|\vec r| \le 1$. Pure states lie on the surface of the Bloch sphere,
and mixed states inside it, in the *Bloch ball*. At the centre lies the maximally mixed
state $I/2$, a uniformly random bit. The purity is $\Tr[\rho^2] = (1+|\vec r|^2)/2$: 1
on the sphere, and $1/2$ at the centre.

The same decomposition works for any number of qubits, with Pauli strings in place of
Pauli matrices:
$$
\rho = \frac{1}{2^n}\sum_{P} \langle P\rangle\, P ,
$$ {#eq-pauli-expansion}
where the sum runs over all $4^n$ Pauli strings on $n$ qubits, and $\langle I\rangle = 1$.
To see why, note two facts. The product of two Pauli strings is, up to a factor, another Pauli
string, which is the identity only if the two are equal. And every Pauli string
other than the identity has trace zero. So $\Tr[PQ] = 2^n$ if $P = Q$ and $0$ otherwise:
the $4^n$ Pauli strings are orthogonal, and they form a basis of all $2^n\times 2^n$
matrices. Multiplying the right-hand side of @eq-pauli-expansion by a Pauli string $Q$
and taking the trace keeps only the term $P = Q$, and gives
$\Tr[Q\rho] = \langle Q\rangle$, as it should. The expectation values of the Pauli
strings fix the state, as the Bloch vector does for one qubit, and most of this chapter
follows what noise does to them. To describe some of the qubits on their own, we
discard the others with the *partial trace*, defined by
$\Tr_B[A\otimes B] = \Tr[B]\,A$. In @eq-pauli-expansion, it keeps the terms whose Pauli
strings act as the identity on the discarded qubits.

### Quantum channels {#sec-kraus}

Noise turns one density matrix into another. The maps that describe this are called
quantum channels.

::: {#def-channel}
## Quantum channel
A [quantum channel]{.gloss key="quantum-channel"} maps a density matrix $\rho$ to
$$
\Lambda(\rho) = \sum_k K_k\, \rho\, K_k^\dagger , \qquad \text{with} \quad \sum_k K_k^\dagger K_k = I .
$$ {#eq-kraus}
The matrices $K_k$ are its [Kraus operators]{.gloss key="kraus-operators"}.
:::

Each Kraus operator describes one thing that can happen to the qubit, with probability
$\Tr[K_k\rho K_k^\dagger]$. The condition on the Kraus operators keeps the trace, since
$\Tr[\Lambda(\rho)] = \Tr\big[\sum_k K_k^\dagger K_k\,\rho\big] = \Tr[\rho]$, so these
probabilities sum to one. Each term
$K_k\rho K_k^\dagger$ is also positive semidefinite, so $\Lambda(\rho)$ is again a density
matrix. This still holds if the channel acts on only some of the qubits of a larger system,
a property called [complete positivity]{.gloss key="completely-positive"}. It is
stronger than positivity: the transpose, for example, is positive but not completely
positive. Conversely, every linear map that is completely positive and keeps the trace
(CPTP) has a Kraus form. More details, with proofs, can be found in @nielsen2010
[sec. 8.2] and in the Quantum Information Theory notes of @walter2025 [Theorem 5.3 and
Lemma 5.5, where the Kraus operators are called $X_i$].

Where do channels come from? A qubit is never perfectly isolated (@sec-qubit-needs): it
interacts with its environment, for example with defects in the chip
(@sec-noise-sources). Qubit and environment together evolve unitarily, but we do not keep
track of the environment, so we discard it with the partial trace. The result is always a
channel on the qubit. Conversely, every channel can arise in this way, and the unitary and the
environment that produce it are called a *Stinespring dilation* of the channel.
@exr-environment works out an example, and more details can be found in @walter2025
[sec. 5.2].

A unitary gate $U$ is a channel with the single Kraus operator $U$. Applying $\Lambda_1$
and then $\Lambda_2$ gives a channel with the Kraus operators $K^{(2)}_j K^{(1)}_k$. And
if $\Lambda_i$ happens with probability $p_i$, the mixture $\sum_i p_i\Lambda_i(\rho)$ is
a channel with the Kraus operators $\sqrt{p_i}\,K^{(i)}_k$. Most noise in this chapter is
of this last kind: with some probability, something goes wrong.

## Noise on one qubit {#sec-single-qubit-noise}

### Pauli channels on the Bloch sphere {#sec-pauli-channels}

The simplest errors are Pauli matrices: $X$ flips the bit, $Z$ flips the sign of the
relative phase between $\ket{0}$ and $\ket{1}$, and $Y$ does both.

::: {#def-pauli-channel}
## Pauli channel
A [Pauli channel]{.gloss key="pauli-channel"} on one qubit applies the error
$Q \in \{I, X, Y, Z\}$ with probability $q_Q$:
$$
\Lambda(\rho) = q_I\,\rho + q_X\, X\rho X + q_Y\, Y\rho Y + q_Z\, Z\rho Z,
\qquad q_I + q_X + q_Y + q_Z = 1 .
$$
Its Kraus operators are $K_Q = \sqrt{q_Q}\,Q$, for $Q \in \{I, X, Y, Z\}$.
:::

What does a Pauli channel do to the Bloch vector? Conjugating a Pauli matrix by another
gives back the same matrix, up to a sign: $QPQ = P$ if $Q = I$ or $Q = P$, and
$QPQ = -P$ otherwise, because different Pauli matrices anticommute. The channel
therefore maps each Pauli matrix to a multiple of itself, $\Lambda(X) = f_x X$, and
likewise for $Y$ and $Z$, with
$$
\begin{aligned}
f_x &= q_I + q_X - q_Y - q_Z , \\
f_y &= q_I - q_X + q_Y - q_Z , \\
f_z &= q_I - q_X - q_Y + q_Z ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-pauli-factors}
while $\Lambda(I) = I$. By @eq-bloch, the channel multiplies each component of the
Bloch vector by its own factor, $r_j \mapsto f_j r_j$, and so each expectation value:
$\langle X\rangle \mapsto f_x\langle X\rangle$, and so on. We call $f_x$, $f_y$ and
$f_z$ the *shrinking factors* of the channel. They are the main tool of this chapter: as
long as the noise is a Pauli channel, its effect on a measured expectation value is a
multiplication. In the Bloch ball, a Pauli channel squeezes the ball into an ellipsoid
with semi-axes $|f_x|$, $|f_y|$ and $|f_z|$, centred at the maximally mixed state.

### Depolarising and dephasing noise {#sec-depolarising-dephasing}

Two Pauli channels describe most of the noise on a single qubit in this chapter.

::: {#def-depolarising}
## Depolarising and dephasing channels
The [depolarising channel]{.gloss key="depolarising"} on one qubit is the Pauli channel
with $q_X = q_Y = q_Z = p/4$:
$$
\Lambda(\rho) = \Big(1 - \frac{3p}{4}\Big)\rho + \frac{p}{4}\big(X\rho X + Y\rho Y + Z\rho Z\big) .
$$
The [dephasing channel]{.gloss key="dephasing-channel"} is the Pauli channel with
$q_Z = p$:
$$
\Lambda(\rho) = (1-p)\,\rho + p\, Z\rho Z .
$$
:::

The depolarising channel treats the three axes alike. By @eq-pauli-factors, its factors
are $f_x = f_y = f_z = 1 - p$. It shrinks the Bloch ball uniformly towards its centre
(@fig-bloch-pauli a), and every expectation value with it:
$\langle P\rangle \mapsto (1-p)\langle P\rangle$. By @eq-bloch, the state with the
Bloch vector $(1-p)\vec r$ is the mixture $(1-p)\rho + p\,I/2$, so
$$
\Lambda(\rho) = (1-p)\,\rho + p\,\frac{I}{2} :
$$ {#eq-depolarising}
with probability $p$, the depolarising channel replaces the state by the maximally mixed
state. This form gives other Kraus operators: $\sqrt{1-p}\,I$ and the four matrices
$\sqrt{p/2}\,\ket{i}\bra{j}$ with $i, j \in \{0, 1\}$. The same channel can therefore have
different Kraus operators. The depolarising channel also commutes with every single-qubit unitary
$U$: $U\Lambda(\rho)U^\dagger = (1-p)\,U\rho U^\dagger + p\,I/2 = \Lambda(U\rho U^\dagger)$,
since $U(I/2)U^\dagger = I/2$.

The dephasing channel has the factors $f_x = f_y = 1 - 2p$ and $f_z = 1$. It leaves
$\langle Z\rangle$, and with it the probabilities of measuring 0 and 1, unchanged. It
shrinks the components of the Bloch vector in the $xy$ plane, which carry the relative
phase between $\ket{0}$ and $\ket{1}$. The ball is squeezed towards the $z$ axis
(@fig-bloch-pauli b), and for $p = 1/2$ it collapses onto it. It is also called the
[phase-flip channel]{.gloss key="phase-flip"}, after its Kraus form, a $Z$ error with
probability $p$. The name suggests a phase that now and then flips suddenly, but
dephasing usually comes from a gradual loss of information about the phase, as we see
below.

![The Bloch sphere (grey) and its image (blue) under two Pauli channels. The dots mark where $\ket{0}$ and $\ket{1}$ go. (a) Depolarising noise shrinks the ball uniformly, and (b) dephasing squeezes it towards the $z$ axis.](figures/bloch-pauli-channels){#fig-bloch-pauli width=70%}

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
In the widget below, set the probabilities $q_X$, $q_Y$ and $q_Z$ of a Pauli channel and
see how it deforms the Bloch ball: for example, $q_X = q_Y = q_Z$ for depolarising
noise, or only $q_Z$ for dephasing. Drag the picture to turn the view.

{{< include _pauli-widget.qmd >}}
:::

**The physical origin of dephasing.** The relative phase of a superposition $\alpha\ket{0} + \beta\ket{1}$ turns at a rate set
by the qubit's frequency (@sec-noise-sources), and the device is calibrated to expect
this. Suppose that the frequency of the qubit is shifted by a small amount $\delta$ (in radians per
second), for example by a fluctuating magnetic field. The qubit then picks up an extra phase
that nobody expected: in a time $t$, its relative phase turns by an extra angle
$\theta = \delta t$. This is the rotation $R_Z(\theta)$ of @eq-rx-rz. If we knew
$\delta$, we could undo this rotation. If we do not know it, we do not know $\theta$
either, and the qubit undergoes a random rotation. Its state becomes the mixture
$\Lambda(\rho) = \mathbb{E}\big[R_Z(\theta)\,\rho\,R_Z(\theta)^\dagger\big]$, where
$\mathbb{E}$ is the average over $\theta$. By @exr-virtual-z,
$R_Z(\theta)XR_Z(\theta)^\dagger = \cos\theta\, X + \sin\theta\, Y$. For an angle that
is as likely to be positive as negative, the sines average to zero:
$$
\Lambda(X) = \mathbb{E}[\cos\theta]\, X, \qquad
\Lambda(Y) = \mathbb{E}[\cos\theta]\, Y, \qquad
\Lambda(Z) = Z .
$$
These are the factors of a dephasing channel with $1 - 2p = \mathbb{E}[\cos\theta]$: an
unknown phase acts as dephasing. The longer the qubit waits, the wider the spread of
$\theta = \delta t$, and the more information about the phase is lost. Once the spread
is much larger than a radian, $\mathbb{E}[\cos\theta]$ is close to zero and $p$ close to
$1/2$: the phase is lost. For a Gaussian angle with variance $\sigma^2$,
$\mathbb{E}[\cos\theta] = e^{-\sigma^2/2}$ (@exr-random-phase).

::: {#exr-random-phase}
## Random phases
A qubit undergoes the rotation $R_Z(\theta)$, where $\theta$ is a Gaussian random angle
with mean zero and variance $\sigma^2$.

(a) Show that $\mathbb{E}[\cos\theta] = e^{-\sigma^2/2}$.

    :::: {.hint}
    $\cos\theta$ is the real part of $e^{i\theta}$.
    ::::

(b) Which dephasing probability $p$ does this channel have? What is it for
$\sigma \ll 1$?
:::

### Noise gate by gate {#sec-noisy-circuits}

A common approximation of the noise on a device models each noisy gate as the ideal gate
$U$ followed by a channel $\Lambda$, so that it maps $\rho$ to $\Lambda(U\rho U^\dagger)$.
A circuit of noisy gates is then a composition of channels. Quantum software development
kits (SDKs), such as the Qiskit of the tutorials, usually describe noise in this way.
The approximation assumes that the noise has no memory: the channel
after each gate does not depend on what happened before. Noise of this kind is called
[Markovian]{.gloss key="markovian"}. @sec-slow-noise describes the main exception. The
shrinking factors make compositions easy: two Pauli channels in a row multiply each
expectation value by the factors of both.

::: {#exr-composition}
## Composing depolarising channels
(a) Apply the depolarising channel with parameter $p_1$ and then the one with $p_2$,
using @eq-depolarising. Show that the result is again a depolarising
channel, and check that its factor is $(1-p_1)(1-p_2)$.

(b) A qubit is prepared in $\ket{+}$, and $n$ noisy $X$ gates are applied, each followed
by depolarising noise with parameter $p$. What is $\langle X\rangle$ at the end? For
$p = 10^{-3}$, after how many gates has $\langle X\rangle$ fallen to half of its
initial value?

    :::: {.hint}
    Where in the circuit can the channels be moved?
    ::::

(c) Two qubits each undergo depolarising noise with parameter $p$, independently, so
that the channel on both is $\Lambda\otimes\Lambda$. By which factors do
$\langle Z\otimes I\rangle$ and $\langle Z\otimes Z\rangle$ shrink? Do these factors
depend on the state of the two qubits?

    :::: {.hint}
    A product of channels acts factor by factor:
    $(\Lambda\otimes\Lambda)(A\otimes B) = \Lambda(A)\otimes\Lambda(B)$.
    ::::
:::

### Relaxation and non-unital noise {#sec-relaxation}

The channels so far are Pauli channels, and they share a property: they map the
maximally mixed state to itself, $\Lambda(I/2) = I/2$, so the centre of the Bloch ball
stays where it is. A channel with this property is called
[unital]{.gloss key="unital"}. Unital noise can only make a state more mixed: it
destroys information, but it does not push the qubit towards any particular state.

[Relaxation]{.gloss key="relaxation"}, the decay of $\ket{1}$ to $\ket{0}$
(@sec-noise-sources), is different. A qubit in $\ket{1}$ gives its energy to the
environment and ends up in $\ket{0}$. Relaxation therefore pushes every state towards
$\ket{0}$, the maximally mixed state included: it is not unital. It is described by the
[amplitude-damping]{.gloss key="amplitude-damping"} channel, with the Kraus operators
$$
K_0 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{1-\gamma} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
K_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \sqrt{\gamma} \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \sqrt{\gamma}\,\ket{0}\bra{1} .
$$ {#eq-amplitude-damping}
$K_1$ is the decay itself: a qubit in $\ket{1}$ jumps to $\ket{0}$, with probability
$\gamma$. $K_0$ is the case without a decay, which also shrinks the amplitude of
$\ket{1}$, since a qubit that has not decayed is more likely to have been in $\ket{0}$
all along. Applied to a density matrix, the channel gives
$$
\begin{pmatrix} \rho_{00} & \rho_{01} \\ \rho_{10} & \rho_{11} \end{pmatrix} \mapsto
\begin{pmatrix} \rho_{00} + \gamma\rho_{11} & \sqrt{1-\gamma}\,\rho_{01} \\
\sqrt{1-\gamma}\,\rho_{10} & (1-\gamma)\,\rho_{11} \end{pmatrix} .
$$
In terms of the Bloch vector, $r_z \mapsto (1-\gamma)\,r_z + \gamma$ and
$r_{x,y} \mapsto \sqrt{1-\gamma}\, r_{x,y}$: the ball shrinks, and its centre moves
towards $\ket{0}$, to $r_z = \gamma$ (@fig-bloch-t1t2 a). Non-unital noise can thus make
a state purer: for $\gamma = 1$, even the maximally mixed state becomes the pure state
$\ket{0}$.

### Relaxation ($T_1$) and dephasing ($T_2^*$) times {#sec-t1-t2}

Two experiments measure how fast a qubit relaxes and dephases, and define two of the
times that providers quote for their devices (@sec-noise-sources).

::: {#def-t1}
## Relaxation time $T_1$
Prepare a qubit in $\ket{1}$ and wait for a time $t$: the probability of still finding
it in $\ket{1}$ decays as $e^{-t/T_1}$. $T_1$ is called the *relaxation time*.
:::

::: {#def-t2-star}
## Dephasing time $T_2^*$
Prepare a qubit in $\ket{+}$ and wait for a time $t$: its
[coherence]{.gloss key="coherence"}, the size $|\rho_{01}|$ of the off-diagonal entry of
its density matrix, decays approximately as $e^{-t/T_2^*}$.
[$T_2^*$]{.gloss key="t2-star"} is called the *dephasing time*. It is measured with a
[Ramsey experiment]{.gloss key="ramsey"} (@fig-ramsey-echo a): a $\pi/2$ pulse turns
$\ket{0}$ into $\ket{+}$, and after the wait, a second $\pi/2$ pulse turns the $x$
component of the Bloch vector into the $z$ component, which the measurement reads out.
:::

Which channels produce these two laws? For $T_1$, it is amplitude damping: after a time
$t$, the probability $\rho_{11}$ of finding $\ket{1}$ has decayed by $1-\gamma$, so
$\gamma = 1 - e^{-t/T_1}$. Amplitude damping also shrinks the coherence, by
$\sqrt{1-\gamma} = e^{-t/2T_1}$. Even without dephasing, relaxation therefore limits
the coherence: for a pure state $\alpha\ket{0} + \beta\ket{1}$, the coherence is
$|\alpha\beta|$, and the amplitude $\beta$ decays at half the rate of the probability
$|\beta|^2$.

The rest of the decay is dephasing, caused by the unknown phases of
@sec-depolarising-dephasing. The qubit frequency is shifted by an amount that we do not know, so
the phase drifts by an angle that we do not know, and after some time the information
about the phase is lost. We describe this by a dephasing channel whose factor decays as
$1 - 2p = e^{-t/T_\varphi}$. This is called [pure dephasing]{.gloss key="pure-dephasing"},
to distinguish it from the loss of coherence caused by relaxation. Its time $T_\varphi$ is
called the pure-dephasing time. Amplitude damping and dephasing commute (@exr-t1-t2), and the
coherence decays with both factors, $e^{-t/2T_1}e^{-t/T_\varphi} = e^{-t/T_2^*}$, where
$$
\frac{1}{T_2^*} = \frac{1}{2T_1} + \frac{1}{T_\varphi} .
$$ {#eq-t2}
@fig-bloch-t1t2 b shows the combined channel.

Since $1/T_\varphi \ge 0$, @eq-t2 gives $T_2^* \le 2T_1$. This bound matters in
practice. The dephasing channel needs $T_\varphi$, but $T_\varphi$ cannot be measured on
its own, because relaxation cannot be switched off: every measurement of the coherence
includes the decay $e^{-t/2T_1}$. Experiments measure $T_1$ and $T_2^*$, and
$T_\varphi$ follows from @eq-t2. A noise model built from measured values therefore
needs $T_2^* \le 2T_1$. Otherwise, $1/T_\varphi$ would be negative, and the dephasing
channel would need $p < 0$, which is not a channel. The simulators of SDKs reject or
correct such values.

![The Bloch sphere (grey) and its image (blue) under (a) amplitude damping, which shrinks the ball and pulls it towards $\ket{0}$, and (b) an idle qubit, with relaxation and pure dephasing together, after a wait $t = T_1/2$ with $T_2^* = T_1/2$. The dots mark where $\ket{0}$ and $\ket{1}$ go.](figures/bloch-relaxation-dephasing){#fig-bloch-t1t2 width=70%}

An idle qubit undergoes this combined channel while it waits. For a short wait $t$, its
factors are $1 - t/T_2^*$ on the $x$ and $y$ axes and $1 - t/T_1$ on the $z$ axis, so
its error is of order $t/T_2^*$ (@sec-budgets makes this precise). A wait of 100 ns
with $T_2^* = 100$ µs therefore costs as much as a single-qubit gate, or more. @tbl-channels
collects the single-qubit channels.

| Channel | Pauli errors | $f_x = f_y$ | $f_z$ | Centre of the ball | Describes |
|--------------------|--------------------------|-----------|---------|---------------|---------------|
| depolarising | $X$, $Y$ and $Z$, each with probability $p/4$ | $1-p$ | $1-p$ | fixed | gate errors |
| dephasing | $Z$ with probability $p$ | $1-2p$ | $1$ | fixed | unknown phases ($T_\varphi$) |
| amplitude damping | not a Pauli channel (@eq-amplitude-damping) | $\sqrt{1-\gamma}$ | $1-\gamma$ | moves to $r_z = \gamma$ | relaxation ($T_1$) |

: Single-qubit channels. The factors multiply the components of the Bloch vector. For an idle qubit, $\gamma = 1 - e^{-t/T_1}$ and $1 - 2p = e^{-t/T_\varphi}$. {#tbl-channels}

(a) Show that amplitude damping and dephasing commute. Write the Bloch vector of
$\ket{+}$ after it has been idle for a time $t$.

    :::: {.hint}
    Compare what the two channels do to $\rho_{00}$, $\rho_{11}$ and $\rho_{01}$.

(b) Suppose the calibration data of a superconducting device give, for three of its
qubits, $T_1 = 150$, $80$ and $200$ µs and $T_2^* = 120$, $150$ and $60$ µs.
Compute $T_\varphi$ for each qubit. Which process limits the coherence of each,
relaxation or dephasing?
:::

### Echoes and $T_2$ {#sec-slow-noise}

The dephasing channel describes a phase that we do not know: the frequency shift
$\delta$ of @sec-depolarising-dephasing, and with it the angle $\theta = \delta t$, differs from
shot to shot by an amount that we cannot predict. Physically, this is a reasonable
picture when the frequency fluctuates slowly, so that $\delta$ stays constant during each
shot. But then the qubit picks up its unknown phase at a steady rate, and there is an
easy way to undo it. An $X$ pulse halfway through the wait exchanges $\ket{0}$ and
$\ket{1}$, which reverses the sign of the phase picked up so far. The second half
of the wait then undoes the first, whatever the value of $\delta$ (@exr-echo). This is called
an [echo]{.gloss key="echo"}, or Hahn echo, after Erwin Hahn, who found it with nuclear
spins in 1950. It leaves the qubit flipped, so a second $X$ is added at
the end of the wait. Repeated echoes during a long wait, called
[dynamical decoupling]{.gloss key="dynamical-decoupling"}, protect idle qubits from slow
noise on the device itself, while the error mitigation of later chapters corrects the
estimates after the run.

If the frequency also changes during the wait, the phases picked up in the two halves
differ, and the echo cancels only the part they have in common. What is left comes from
fluctuations on timescales shorter than the wait. The angle is then a sum of many small,
independent kicks, one for each short interval, so it is Gaussian (by the central limit
theorem). Its variance is the sum of the variances of the kicks, the fact behind
@eq-standard-error, and it therefore grows in proportion to $t$. We write it
as $\sigma^2 = 2t/T_\varphi$, so that the coherence decays as
$e^{-\sigma^2/2} = e^{-t/T_\varphi}$. Fast noise gives the exponential decay of pure
dephasing that @sec-t1-t2 assumed.

An echo experiment, a Ramsey experiment with an $X$ pulse halfway and another at the end
of the wait (@fig-ramsey-echo),
therefore measures a longer time than $T_2^*$, called $T_2$: the decay due to relaxation
and fast noise only. It obeys @eq-t2 with $T_2$ in place of $T_2^*$ and a longer
$T_\varphi$, so $T_2^* \le T_2 \le 2T_1$. The star of $T_2^*$ marks the time that
includes slow noise. Dynamical decoupling is usually assumed to be available for idle
qubits, so calibration data often quote $T_2$ rather than $T_2^*$, and the error budgets
of @sec-budgets use $T_2$ too. In a Ramsey experiment, slow noise makes the coherence decay
faster, and the decay need not be exponential: for a frequency shift that is constant
within each shot and Gaussian across shots, it is a Gaussian in $t$ (@exr-echo).

![(a) A Ramsey experiment and an echo. Each $\pi/2$ pulse is a rotation by $\pi/2$ about an axis in the $xy$ plane, and M is the measurement. (b) The coherence left after a wait $t$. With slow noise, the Ramsey signal decays faster than the echo signal, which decays as $e^{-t/T_2}$. The curves are an illustration, with slow noise of one fixed strength.](figures/ramsey-echo){#fig-ramsey-echo width=95%}

Slow noise has memory, so it is the main exception to the Markovian model of
@sec-noisy-circuits. A common source is a defect in the chip that switches between two
states and makes the qubit frequency jump
([random telegraph noise]{.gloss key="telegraph-noise"}). Many such defects give noise in
which slow fluctuations dominate ([1/f noise]{.gloss key="one-over-f"}, with $f$ the
frequency of the fluctuations).

::: {#exr-echo}
## The echo
(a) Show that $X R_Z(\theta) X = R_Z(-\theta)$, and that
$R_Z(\theta/2)\, X\, R_Z(\theta/2) = X$ for every angle $\theta$. An echo on an idle
qubit ends with a second $X$. Why does this second $X$ cost nothing extra when the next
gate on the qubit is a single-qubit gate?

    :::: {.hint}
    Use $XZX = -Z$ and @eq-conjugation. For the second $X$, see @sec-virtual-z.
    ::::

(b) In a Ramsey experiment, the qubit frequency is shifted by an amount $\delta$ that is
constant within each shot, and Gaussian with standard deviation $\sigma_\delta$
across shots. Ignoring relaxation and fast noise, show that the coherence after a wait
$t$ is $e^{-\sigma_\delta^2 t^2/2}$. What is it with an echo?

    Use @exr-random-phase with $\theta = \delta t$.
    ::::
:::

## Noise on many qubits {#sec-multi-qubit-noise}

On many qubits, the tools of @sec-pauli-channels carry over with one more fact of Pauli
algebra. Two Pauli strings $P$ and $Q$ either commute, $PQ = QP$, or anticommute, $PQ = -QP$; we
can summarise this by defining the sign $s_{PQ} = \pm 1$ such that $PQ = s_{PQ}\,QP$. A Pauli channel on $n$ qubits, $\Lambda(\rho) = \sum_Q q_Q\, Q\rho Q$, therefore
multiplies the expectation value of every Pauli string $P$ by its own factor,
$$
\langle P\rangle \mapsto f_P\langle P\rangle, \qquad f_P = \sum_Q s_{PQ}\, q_Q .
$$ {#eq-pauli-factors-n}

Noise that acts on each qubit separately, with a channel $\Lambda_j$ on qubit $j$, is
called *local*: the channel on all qubits is $\Lambda_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\Lambda_n$. It
acts factor by factor on a Pauli string and leaves the identity factors unchanged, so the
factor of a string is the product of the single-qubit factors at its non-identity
positions.

As examples, we extend the simplest noise of @sec-depolarising-dephasing, the depolarising
channel, to many qubits. There are two natural ways to do this.

::: {#def-local-depolarising}
## Local depolarising noise
[Local depolarising noise]{.gloss key="local-depolarising"} with parameter $p$ applies
the depolarising channel of @def-depolarising to each qubit, independently.
:::

::: {#def-global-depolarising}
## Global depolarising noise
The [global depolarising channel]{.gloss key="global-depolarising"} on $n$ qubits replaces
the state of all qubits by the maximally mixed state with probability $p$:
$$
\Lambda(\rho) = (1-p)\,\rho + p\,\frac{I}{2^n} .
$$
:::

For $n = 1$, both are the depolarising channel of @eq-depolarising. With local
depolarising noise, a Pauli string of [weight]{.gloss key="weight"} $w$, its number of
non-identity positions, shrinks by $(1-p)^w$: strings of high weight lose their signal
fastest.

Global depolarising behaves differently. Compare the Kraus forms first. With
local depolarising noise, each qubit independently
suffers $X$, $Y$ or $Z$ with probability $p/4$ each, so an error on $w$ given qubits has a
probability of order $(p/4)^w$: errors on many qubits at once are rare. The global channel
is a Pauli channel too. Averaging $Q\rho Q$ over all $4^n$ Pauli strings $Q$ gives
$I/2^n$. Indeed, by @eq-pauli-factors-n, the factor of every non-identity string $P$
vanishes: at a position where $P$ is not the identity, two of the four choices of $Q$
anticommute with it, so half of all strings do. So
$$
(1-p)\,\rho + p\,\frac{I}{2^n} = \Big(1 - p + \frac{p}{4^n}\Big)\rho + \frac{p}{4^n}\sum_{Q\ne I} Q\rho Q .
$$
All $4^n - 1$ non-identity errors are equally likely, and an error on all $n$ qubits is
as likely as an error on one. As a result, global depolarising shrinks every Pauli string
by the same factor, $1-p$, whatever its weight. No product of local channels does this:
it would need $f_{ZI} = f_{IZ} = f_{ZZ} = 1-p$, while a product gives
$f_{ZZ} = f_{ZI}\, f_{IZ}$.

Like its single-qubit version, global depolarising noise commutes with every unitary,
here on all $n$ qubits. If
every gate $i$ of a circuit is followed by global depolarising noise with parameter
$p_i$, all of it can be moved to the end of the circuit. Every expectation value then shrinks by the
same factor:
$$
\langle P\rangle \mapsto f\langle P\rangle, \qquad f = \prod_i (1-p_i) .
$$ {#eq-global-factor}
A single number describes the noise of the whole circuit. This makes global depolarising
noise much easier to model than local noise, and to correct for (@sec-rescaling).

Local noise does not commute with entangling gates. Conjugation by CZ turns an $X$ on the
second qubit into $Z\otimes X$ (@sec-compiling), so an $X$ error before a CZ is a
two-qubit error after it. Errors therefore spread through a circuit: each later two-qubit gate
can carry an error to one more qubit, and the qubits that it can reach form a cone, called
its *light cone* (@fig-error-spreading). For deep circuits of random gates, global
depolarising noise is then a good approximation of local noise. These circuits are called
[scrambling]{.gloss key="scrambling"}: the light cone of every error soon covers all the
qubits, so that any error, wherever it happens, leaves the output close to random. Global
depolarising noise is therefore a very useful model for estimates
(@sec-fidelity and @sec-bias-variance), although real noise is mostly local.

![One error (star) in the brick-wall circuit of @exr-error-budget, on qubit $q_4$ after the pulse of the second layer. The shaded wires are its light cone: the qubits that the later CZ gates can carry it to. By the last layers, it can reach every qubit.](figures/error-spreading){#fig-error-spreading width=60%}

[Correlated errors]{.gloss key="correlated-errors"} affect several qubits together. An
example is [crosstalk]{.gloss key="crosstalk"} (@sec-superconducting), including the
coupling between neighbouring superconducting qubits that is never fully off and acts as
a small, unwanted $R_{ZZ}$ rotation (@eq-rzz). Some correlated errors affect a whole
chip. When a cosmic ray, or the radioactive decay of a trace impurity, deposits energy in
a superconducting chip, the energy spreads as vibrations of the crystal
([phonons]{.gloss key="phonon"}), and for tens of milliseconds all qubits on the chip
relax much faster than usual. In the experiment of @mcewen2022, this happened about once
every ten seconds. Such bursts break the independence of errors that the estimates of
@sec-fidelity assume, and they matter most for error correction.

## Noisy gates {#sec-gate-errors}

In @sec-noisy-circuits, we modelled the noisy gates of a device as ideal gates, each
followed by a channel. But which channel is the right one? Part of it is the
relaxation and dephasing during the gate. The rest comes from the
control: the pulses that implement a gate are never exactly right.

A [coherent error]{.gloss key="coherent-error"} (@sec-noise-sources) is a fixed, wrong
unitary. A pulse that is slightly too strong, for example, implements
$R_X(\theta+\eta) = R_X(\eta)R_X(\theta)$ instead of $R_X(\theta)$: the channel after the
gate is the unitary $R_X(\eta)$. Biased angles in parametrised gates return with
variational algorithms. <!-- VQE-LINK: link "variational algorithms" to the variational
chapter. --> An [incoherent error]{.gloss key="incoherent-error"} is random: the error
unitary differs from shot to shot, and averages to a channel, as the random $R_Z$ did in
@sec-depolarising-dephasing.

The difference matters when a gate is repeated. Apply an $X$ gate $n$ times to a qubit
that starts in $\ket{0}$, each time over-rotated about the $x$ axis by a small angle
$\eta_k$. The result is $X^n$ followed by $R_X(\sum_k\eta_k)$. A total error angle
$\theta$ gives the wrong outcome with probability $\sin^2(\theta/2)$. We use this *error
probability* as the measure of error until @sec-fidelity. If the error is the same every
time, $\eta_k = \eta$, the angles add up like the slow noise of @sec-slow-noise, and the
error probability is $\sin^2(n\eta/2) \approx n^2\eta^2/4$. If the errors are random and
independent, with mean zero and variance $\sigma^2$, they add up like the fast noise
there: the variance of the total angle is $n\sigma^2$, and the average error
probability is about $n\sigma^2/4$. For the same error per gate, $\eta = \sigma$, the
coherent error after $n$ gates is $n$ times larger (@fig-coherent-incoherent).

![The error probability after $n$ over-rotated gates, with the same error per gate: a fixed angle $\eta = 0.02$ (orange) and independent random angles with standard deviation $\sigma = 0.02$ (blue). On these logarithmic axes, the coherent error grows with slope 2 and the incoherent one with slope 1.](figures/coherent-incoherent){#fig-coherent-incoherent width=55%}

Three consequences matter later:

1. The error budgets of @sec-fidelity assume incoherent errors, so they underestimate
   coherent ones.
2. Circuits that repeat identical layers, such as those for time evolution, are the
   worst case.
3. Coherent errors can be made incoherent on purpose: random Pauli gates before and
   after a gate such as CZ, chosen so that they cancel in the ideal circuit, average its
   error into a Pauli channel. This is called [twirling]{.gloss key="twirling"}.
   Each random Pauli gate can be merged with the single-qubit gate next to it, which
   costs a single pulse anyway (@sec-virtual-z), so twirling needs no extra pulses.
   @exr-over-rotation (b) shows the simplest case.

[Leakage]{.gloss key="leakage"} falls outside this description: it takes a qubit out of
its two levels, for example into the third level of a transmon (@fig-energy-levels), so
that channels on $2\times 2$ density matrices cannot describe it.

::: {#exr-over-rotation}
## Coherent and incoherent errors
(a) A gate has a coherent over-rotation of $\eta = 0.01$. After how many repetitions is
the error probability 1%? Answer the same question for random over- and
under-rotations, with mean zero and standard deviation $\sigma = 0.01$.

(b) An $R_X(\theta)$ gate has a small coherent error: it applies $R_Z(\eta)$ after the intended rotation.
For each repetition of the gate, independently and with probability $1/2$, we add a perfect
$X$ gate just before it and another just after it. Since $X$ commutes with $R_X(\theta)$,
the ideal gate is unchanged, but the error becomes $X R_Z(\eta) X$. Show that, averaged over these
random choices, the error of each gate becomes a dephasing channel with $p = \sin^2(\eta/2)$.
How does it now add up over $n$ repetitions?

:::

## Readout errors {#sec-readout-errors}

A measurement can report the wrong bit (@tbl-noise). We describe this with the
[confusion matrix]{.gloss key="confusion-matrix"} $M$, whose entry
$M_{ij} = p(\text{read } i \mid \text{state } j)$ is the probability of reading $i$ when
the qubit is in $\ket{j}$. On one qubit,
$$
M = \begin{pmatrix} 1-e_0 & e_1 \\ e_0 & 1-e_1 \end{pmatrix},
$$
where $e_0 = p(1\mid 0)$ and $e_1 = p(0\mid 1)$ are the two error rates. If we call
reading 1 a positive, $e_0$ is the rate of false positives and $e_1$ the rate of false
negatives. $M$ maps the
probabilities of the true outcomes to those of the recorded ones, so it is a channel on
classical probabilities [@walter2025, sec. 4.3].

If the two error rates are equal, $e_0 = e_1 = e$, the readout acts as a perfect
measurement after a [bit flip]{.gloss key="bit-flip"}: the Pauli channel that applies $X$
with probability $e$. By @eq-pauli-factors, $\langle Z\rangle$ then shrinks by $1-2e$, as
in @exr-readout-bias. Usually, $e_1 > e_0$. A readout on a
superconducting qubit takes about a microsecond (@tbl-timescales), and a qubit in
$\ket{1}$ can relax during it, with a probability of order 1% for $T_1 = 100$ µs. With
$p_0 = (1+\langle Z\rangle)/2$ and $p_1 = (1-\langle Z\rangle)/2$, the recorded
expectation value is then
$$
\langle Z\rangle_{\text{read}} = (1 - e_0 - e_1)\,\langle Z\rangle + (e_1 - e_0) ,
$$ {#eq-readout}
a shrinking factor and an offset, as for amplitude damping.

Preparation can fail too. A qubit that is thermally excited (@exr-thermal) starts in
$\ket{1}$ instead of $\ket{0}$, and a measurement right after the preparation cannot tell
this apart from a readout error (@exr-readout). Errors in state preparation and
measurement are therefore characterised together, as [SPAM errors]{.gloss key="spam"}.

On $n$ qubits, the confusion matrix is $2^n\times 2^n$: its entry $M_{xy}$ is the
probability of reading the bit string $x$ when the qubits are in the basis state
$\ket{y}$. For independent readouts, it is the tensor product of single-qubit
matrices. If, in addition, each qubit's two error
rates are equal, every qubit of a Pauli string shrinks its expectation value by its own
factor $1 - 2e_j$ (@exr-readout-bias). Otherwise, the offsets of @eq-readout also mix in
the expectation values of shorter strings. Correcting estimates for known readout errors
is the simplest form of error mitigation, which we meet later in the course.

::: {#exr-readout}
## Unequal readout errors
A qubit has the readout error rates $e_0 = 1\%$ and $e_1 = 4\%$.

(a) Which value of $\langle Z\rangle$ is recorded on average for the states $\ket{0}$,
$\ket{1}$ and $\ket{+}$?

(b) Suppose instead that the readout is perfect, but that preparing $\ket{0}$ gives
$\ket{1}$ with probability $e_p$, and that $\ket{1}$ is prepared by a perfect $X$ gate
after that. Which confusion matrix does an experiment that prepares $\ket{0}$ and
$\ket{1}$ and measures them report? Can it tell this situation apart from a readout
error?

(c) Why does the difference between the two situations matter for a circuit with gates
between the preparation and the measurement?

    :::: {.hint}
    Where in the circuit does each error act, and what do the gates do to it?
    ::::
:::

## Fidelity and error budgets {#sec-fidelity}

Providers summarise the quality of each operation by a fidelity (@sec-noise-sources).
In this section, we define fidelities, and we use the error rates that providers quote
for a quick estimate of how much signal a circuit keeps. We work out one example, the
same circuit on two platforms.

### Fidelity of states and gates {#sec-fidelity-def}

::: {#def-fidelity}
## Fidelity
The [state fidelity]{.gloss key="state-fidelity"} of a state $\rho$ with a pure target
state $\ket{\psi}$ is $F = \bra{\psi}\rho\ket{\psi}$. The
[average gate fidelity]{.gloss key="average-gate-fidelity"} $F_{\text{avg}}$ of a noisy
gate is the state fidelity of its output with the ideal output $U\ket{\psi}$, averaged
over all pure input states $\ket{\psi}$. The *error per gate* is
$r = 1 - F_{\text{avg}}$.
:::

The state fidelity is the probability that $\rho$ passes a measurement that asks "is the
state $\ket{\psi}$?". Some texts, including @nielsen2010 and the Quantum Information
Theory notes [@walter2025, sec. 4.2], call $\sqrt{\bra{\psi}\rho\ket{\psi}}$ the fidelity
instead. We use the squared version, as Qiskit does.

For example, after depolarising noise with parameter $p$, every pure state has the
fidelity $1 - p/2$ with the ideal one, so $r = p/2$.

Providers usually quote the error per gate $r$, measured with
[randomised benchmarking]{.gloss key="randomised-benchmarking"}. An error budget needs
instead the probability that an operation goes wrong. For a Pauli channel, this is the
*Pauli error* $\varepsilon = 1 - q_I$, the probability of an error other than the
identity. It is slightly larger than $r$. On $d$ levels ($d = 2^n$ for $n$ qubits),
$$
\varepsilon = \frac{d+1}{d}\, r ,
$$ {#eq-pauli-error}
so $\varepsilon = 3r/2$ for a single-qubit gate and $5r/4$ for a two-qubit gate.
Research papers often quote Pauli errors instead of $r$, so a budget must check which of
the two it uses. A derivation of @eq-pauli-error can be found in @nielsen2002.

### Circuit fidelity and the signal left {#sec-signal-left}

A circuit has many gates, each with a small error. Before we run it, we would like to
know how much of the ideal result survives: by how much a measured expectation value
shrinks, and whether what is left can be seen above the shot noise. Computing this
exactly means simulating the noisy circuit, with a detailed noise model. Instead, we
estimate it from the error rates that providers quote, with a few approximations.

Suppose every gate and idle step $i$ of a circuit suffers a Pauli error with probability
$\varepsilon_i$, independently of the others. The probability that a shot runs without
any error is then
$$
f = \prod_i (1-\varepsilon_i) \approx e^{-\sum_i\varepsilon_i} ,
$$ {#eq-circuit-fidelity}
for small $\varepsilon_i$, as in @sec-nisq and @exr-error-budget. Virtual $Z$ gates add
nothing to the sum (@sec-virtual-z). In a scrambling circuit (@sec-multi-qubit-noise),
any error leaves the output close to random, so the noise acts as global depolarising
noise. Every expectation value then shrinks by the same factor $f$, as in
@eq-global-factor with $p_i \approx \varepsilon_i$. So $f$, the probability of a shot
without an error, is also the fraction of the signal that is left, and approximately the
fidelity of the output state with the ideal one.

Readout errors act after the last gate and do not spread. With equal error rates $e$,
they shrink a Pauli string of weight $w$ by $(1-2e)^w \approx e^{-2ew}$
(@exr-readout-bias). Each qubit of the string therefore adds $2e$ to the sum in
@eq-circuit-fidelity, and the other qubits add nothing.

These estimates assume independent, incoherent errors and a circuit that spreads them.
They are rough, but they are what we use to judge whether a result is plausible. With
$N$ shots, the standard error is about $1/\sqrt{N}$ (@eq-standard-error). A measured
value $f\langle P\rangle$ can therefore be told apart from zero only if
$f|\langle P\rangle|$ is several times larger than $1/\sqrt{N}$.

### Example: error budgets on two platforms {#sec-budgets}

As an example, we estimate how much signal one circuit keeps on a superconducting and on
a trapped-ion device. Take the brick-wall circuit of @exr-error-budget, on a line
of 10 qubits with 8 layers, and estimate $\langle Z\otimes Z\rangle$ on two neighbouring
qubits. Each layer applies an $R_X$ pulse to every qubit, its $R_Z$ being virtual, and
CZs between neighbours: 80 pulses and 36 CZs. We take values that are typical of
current devices (@sec-noise-sources and @tbl-timescales):

- superconducting: Pauli errors of 0.03% per pulse (40 ns), 0.5% per CZ (80 ns) and 1%
  per readout, $T_1 = 150$ µs and $T_2 = 100$ µs;
- trapped ions: 0.01% per pulse (20 µs), 0.2% per two-qubit gate (300 µs) and 0.3% per
  readout, $T_2 = 1$ s and a much longer $T_1$, with all gates run one after another.

Idle qubits contribute too. Over a short wait $t$, the error probability of an idle
qubit is about $t/(2T_2) + t/(4T_1)$, from the factors of @sec-t1-t2. It uses
$T_2$ in place of $T_2^*$, since dynamical decoupling protects the idle qubits
(@sec-slow-noise). On the superconducting device, only the two qubits at the ends of the
line wait, during the CZs of every other layer. On the ion trap, each qubit waits for
about 10 ms of the 12 ms that the gates take. @tbl-budget collects the contributions.

| Contribution to $\sum_i\varepsilon_i$ | Superconducting | Trapped ions |
|---|---|---|
| two-qubit gates | $36 \times 0.5\% = 0.18$ | $36 \times 0.2\% = 0.072$ |
| single-qubit pulses | $80 \times 0.03\% = 0.024$ | $80 \times 0.01\% = 0.008$ |
| idling | 8 waits of 80 ns: $0.004$ | about 100 ms in total: $0.05$ |
| readout of the two qubits | $2 \times 2 \times 1\% = 0.04$ | $2 \times 2 \times 0.3\% = 0.012$ |
| total | $0.25$ | $0.14$ |
| signal left, $f$ | $0.78$ | $0.87$ |
| duration of the gates | about 1 µs | about 12 ms |

: Error budget of the 8-layer brick-wall circuit on 10 qubits, for $\langle Z\otimes Z\rangle$ on two neighbouring qubits, with the values in the text. {#tbl-budget}

On the superconducting device, the two-qubit gates dominate, followed by the readout.
Idling hardly matters, since all qubits are busy in most layers. On the ion trap,
every error rate is lower, but the gates take long and run one after another. Each
qubit therefore waits for most of the shot, and idling costs almost as much as the
two-qubit gates. In general, readout errors dominate wide, shallow circuits and
observables of high weight, while gate errors dominate deep circuits.

The same specifications define a [noise model]{.gloss key="noise-model"} for a
simulator: after each gate, a depolarising channel with the relaxation and dephasing of
its duration, together matching the quoted error; the same relaxation and dephasing on
idle qubits; and a confusion matrix per qubit. Such a model is only as good as the last
calibration (@sec-noise-sources). Tutorial 2 builds such a model in code:
[open the T2 notebook in Colab]({{< var colab >}}/tutorials/tutorial-02/T2-noisy-simulation_qiskit.ipynb).

::: {#exr-visible-signal}

Take the brick-wall circuit of @tbl-budget with $L$ layers instead of 8, and suppose
that the ideal value of $\langle Z\otimes Z\rangle$ is $0.5$. We take $10^4$ shots and
call the signal visible if the measured value is at least three standard errors away
from zero.

(a) Write the signal left, $f$, as a function of $L$ for each platform.

    :::: {.hint}
    Split the contributions of @tbl-budget into a part per layer and a fixed part.
    ::::

(b) What is the largest $L$ with a visible signal on each platform? How long do the
gates of the $10^4$ shots take in total on the ion trap?

(c) Which contribution limits $L$ on each platform? Which improvement would help the

:::

## Bias and shot noise {#sec-bias-variance}

### Mean squared error {#sec-mse}

In @sec-shot-noise, the sample mean $\bar s$ of $N$ shots was an unbiased estimator of
$\langle P\rangle$. With noise, each shot comes from the noisy state, and $\bar s$
averages to $f\langle P\rangle$ instead. Its error now has two parts. The
[bias]{.gloss key="bias"} is the difference between its average and the value we want,
$b = \mathbb{E}[\bar s] - \langle P\rangle = (f-1)\langle P\rangle$. Its variance is
$(1 - f^2\langle P\rangle^2)/N$, the square of @eq-standard-error with
$f\langle P\rangle$ in place of $\langle P\rangle$. The two add up in the
[mean squared error]{.gloss key="mse"}:
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[(\bar s - \langle P\rangle)^2\big] = b^2 + \mathrm{Var}(\bar s)
= (1-f)^2\langle P\rangle^2 + \frac{1 - f^2\langle P\rangle^2}{N} .
$$ {#eq-mse}
To see the first equality, write $\bar s - \langle P\rangle = (\bar s - \mathbb{E}[\bar s]) + b$
and expand the square: the cross term averages to zero. More shots shrink only the
variance, while the bias stays.

The two terms are equal at
$$
N^* = \frac{1 - f^2\langle P\rangle^2}{(1-f)^2\langle P\rangle^2} .
$$
Beyond $N^*$ shots, the bias dominates the error, and more shots hardly help: they
estimate the wrong value more precisely. For the superconducting example of
@tbl-budget, with $f = 0.78$ and $\langle P\rangle = 0.5$, $N^* \approx 70$ shots. A
larger circuit has a smaller $f$, and an even smaller $N^*$.

::: {#exr-shots-stop-helping}
## When more shots stop helping
(a) Show that $N^* \approx (1 - \langle P\rangle^2)/\big(\langle P\rangle^2 (\sum_i\varepsilon_i)^2\big)$
when the total error $\sum_i\varepsilon_i$ of the circuit is small.

(b) For the superconducting brick-wall circuit of @tbl-budget with $L$ layers and
$\langle P\rangle = 0.5$, compute the exact $N^*$ for $L = 1$, 8 and 30. Why are more
shots worth taking on a better device?

(c) @exr-readout-bias (c) compared $10^3$ and $10^5$ shots. Compute $N^*$ there, and
explain the result of that comparison.
:::

### Correcting a known shrinking factor {#sec-rescaling}

If the shrinking factor $f$ is known, the bias can be removed: $\bar s/f$ averages to $\langle P\rangle$. The
price is in the variance. Dividing by $f$ multiplies the standard error by $1/f$, so the
same precision as without noise takes $1/f^2 = e^{2\sum_i\varepsilon_i}$ times as many
shots. The cost grows exponentially with the total error of the circuit. For the
superconducting example, this is a factor of 1.6. For a circuit ten times larger, with
$f \approx 0.08$, it is a factor of about 140. This is the simplest method of error
mitigation, applied to readout errors in @exr-readout-bias (d).

Knowing $f$ is the hard part. For global depolarising noise, every expectation value
shrinks by the same factor, and the error rates of the device give it
(@eq-circuit-fidelity). Readout errors, which act only at the end of the circuit, are
another simple case. For generic circuits and noise models, however, each expectation
value is changed in its own way, and predicting it means simulating the noisy circuit.
A cost in shots of the same kind returns with the other mitigation methods later in the
course.

Two questions follow from here. The observables of real applications, such as the energy
of a physical system, are sums of many Pauli strings, each estimated with its own shots
and its own noise. And the bias need not be accepted: error-mitigation methods estimate
and remove it, at a price in shots.
<!-- L3-LINK: link the two questions to the chapters on observables and on error
mitigation, once the order of L3-L5 is decided. -->

## More exercises {#sec-L2-exercises}

These exercises combine material from several sections of the chapter.

::: {#exr-ghz}
## GHZ states under local and global noise
The GHZ state $(\ket{0\cdots 0} + \ket{1\cdots 1})/\sqrt{2}$ on $n$ qubits has
$\langle X\otimes\cdots\otimes X\rangle = 1$, with $X$ on all qubits, and
$\langle Z\otimes Z\otimes I\otimes\cdots\otimes I\rangle = 1$, with $Z$ on the first
two qubits only.

(a) Each qubit undergoes depolarising noise with parameter $p$. By which factors do the
two expectation values shrink?

(b) Which parameter of the global depolarising channel shrinks
$\langle X\otimes\cdots\otimes X\rangle$ by the same factor? What does it then do to
$\langle Z\otimes Z\otimes I\otimes\cdots\otimes I\rangle$?

(c) How could measurements of these two expectation values show whether the noise on a
GHZ state is closer to local or to global depolarising?
:::

::: {#exr-environment}
## Dephasing from an environment
A qubit in the state $\alpha\ket{0} + \beta\ket{1}$ interacts with an environment qubit
in the state $\cos(\phi/2)\ket{0} + \sin(\phi/2)\ket{1}$ through a CZ gate, after which
the environment is discarded.

(a) Show that the qubit undergoes a dephasing channel with $p = \sin^2(\phi/2)$.

    :::: {.hint}
    With the environment second, $\gate{CZ} = I\otimes\ket{0}\bra{0} + Z\otimes\ket{1}\bra{1}$. Take the partial trace over the environment.
    ::::

(b) The Kraus operators of this channel are $K_e = (I\otimes\bra{e})\,\gate{CZ}\,(I\otimes\ket{E})$
for $e = 0, 1$, where $\ket{E}$ is the initial state of the environment. Compute them,
and compare them with those of @def-pauli-channel.
:::

## Further reading {#sec-L2-reading}

@nielsen2010 [sec. 8.3] treats the channels of this chapter in the same Kraus form, and
the Quantum Information Theory notes [@walter2025, secs. 4.4 and 5.1-5.2] give the
general theory. @krantz2019
describes $T_1$, $T_2$, Ramsey and echo experiments on superconducting qubits.
